title: Colors, Symbols & Visual Design
subtitle: Colour is not decoration. It is the fastest instruction a picture can give you.
objectives: Name the primary, secondary and tertiary colours
Explain warm and cool colours and what each one does
Explain complementary colours and why they intensify each other
Explain what a symbol is and how it differs from a picture
Read the symbolism of the Philippine flag

cards.title: You see colour before you read anything
cards.text: Colour reaches the brain in a fraction of a second. Words take longer. That is why every warning sign is red first.

cards.title: How colours sit against each other
cards.text: Tap each one. The circles are the actual colours, not descriptions of them.

cards.title: Primary, secondary, tertiary
cards.text: Primaries cannot be mixed from anything else. Everything else on the wheel comes from them.
points: **Primary:** red, yellow, blue.
**Secondary:** orange, green, violet.
**Tertiary:** a primary mixed with its neighbour.
**Red-orange and blue-green** are tertiary.

question.text: Which set is the primary colours?
question.explain: In paint, red, yellow and blue cannot be mixed from anything else. Everything else comes from them.

cards.title: Cyberpunk's yellow is a job, not a mood
cards.text: Night City uses hot yellow for anything you can interact with. You learn to scan for it without being told.
points: **Colour teaches you the controls** silently.
**Red still means damage** in almost every game.
**Health bars are green** for the same reason.
**A designer chose all of that.**

cards.title: Warm comes forward, cool falls back
cards.text: Warm colours look closer than they are. Cool colours look further away. Painters use this to build depth on a flat surface.
points: **Warm:** red, orange, yellow. Fire and sun.
**Cool:** blue, green, violet. Water and shade.
**Distant hills are painted bluer** on purpose.
**Nothing moves.** Your eye is being steered.

question.text: Cool colours make an object look closer to the viewer.
question.explain: The opposite. Cool colours recede and warm colours advance. Painters use it to fake distance.

cards.title: Halfway
cards.text: Part 2 is symbols and the flag. Look away from the screen for a moment first.

cards.title: A symbol is a deal between people
cards.text: A picture of a heart looks nothing like the organ. It means love because enough people agreed it does.

cards.title: Resemblance or agreement
cards.text: Some signs look like the thing they stand for. Others only work because you were taught them.
points: **A drawn aeroplane** on a sign resembles a plane.
**A red octagon** resembles nothing. It means stop.
**Learned symbols are stronger** and faster.
**They also stop working** outside their culture.

cards.title: Every badge is a compressed story
cards.text: The Ferrari horse came from an Italian fighter pilot's plane in the First World War. It says nothing about cars.
points: **A badge carries history** you cannot see.
**BMW's roundel** uses Bavarian blue and white.
**Nothing in either shape** looks like an engine.
**Agreement did all the work.**

question.text: Why does a red octagon mean stop?
options: Because people agreed on it and learned it
Because the shape looks like stopping
Because red is the brightest colour
Because octagons are easy to cut
question.explain: Nothing about the shape resembles stopping. Agreement makes the symbol work, and it works fast.

cards.title: Everything on it means something
cards.text: The Philippine flag is a design brief, not a decoration. Each element was chosen to say a specific thing.
points: **Blue** for peace, truth and justice.
**Red** for patriotism and courage.
**White triangle** for equality and fraternity.
**Eight rays** for the first eight provinces to revolt.

cards.title: The flag can be flown upside down
cards.text: Red on top means the country is at war. It is the only national flag in the world designed to be flown two ways.
points: **Blue on top:** peace.
**Red on top:** a state of war.
**The three stars** are Luzon, Visayas and Mindanao.
**The sun** stands for freedom.

question.text: What do the eight rays of the sun on the flag stand for?
options: The first eight provinces to revolt against Spain
question.explain: The three stars are Luzon, Visayas and Mindanao. The eight rays are the first provinces to rise.

cards.title: Design is deciding what to leave out
cards.text: The flag has four elements and no words. A design that tries to say everything ends up saying nothing.
points: **Few elements, each one loaded.**
**It reads at any size**, on any screen.
**It works in one colour** if it has to.
**Those three tests** are what design means.

terms.def: Red, yellow and blue. They cannot be mixed from other colours.
Orange, green and violet. Each is two primaries mixed.
A primary mixed with the secondary beside it, like red-orange.
Opposite on the wheel. Side by side, both look brighter.
Warm colours advance towards the viewer. Cool colours recede.
A mark that stands for an idea because people agreed it does.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **Red, yellow, blue** make everything else.
**Warm advances. Cool recedes.**
**A symbol works by agreement**, not resemblance.
**The flag flies red-up** when the country is at war.

quiz.text: Which of these is a secondary colour?
quiz.explain: Green is blue and yellow mixed. Orange and violet are the other two secondaries.
quiz.objective: Name the primary, secondary and tertiary colours

quiz.text: How is a tertiary colour made?
options: By mixing a primary with the secondary next to it
By adding white to a primary
By adding black to a secondary
quiz.explain: Red-orange and blue-green are tertiary colours made this way.
quiz.objective: Name the primary, secondary and tertiary colours

quiz.explain: Warm colours are the fire and sunlight colours. They appear to come forward.
quiz.objective: Explain warm and cool colours and what each one does

quiz.text: Why do painters use cool colours for distant hills?
options: Cool colours appear to recede, which fakes distance
quiz.explain: It builds depth on a flat surface. Nothing moves; your eye is being steered.
quiz.objective: Explain warm and cool colours and what each one does

options: Colours opposite each other on the wheel
Colours next to each other on the wheel
quiz.explain: Red and green, blue and orange, yellow and violet. Side by side, each looks brighter.
quiz.objective: Explain complementary colours and why they intensify each other

quiz.text: Complementary colours make each other look duller when placed side by side.
quiz.explain: False. They intensify each other. Mixed together is what makes them dull.
quiz.objective: Explain complementary colours and why they intensify each other

options: People agreeing on what it means
Looking exactly like the thing it stands for
quiz.explain: Learned symbols are faster than pictures, and they stop working outside their culture.
quiz.objective: Explain what a symbol is and how it differs from a picture

quiz.text: What do the three stars on the Philippine flag represent?
quiz.explain: The three main island groups. The eight rays are the first provinces to revolt.
quiz.objective: Read the symbolism of the Philippine flag

quiz.text: What does the white triangle stand for?
quiz.explain: Blue is peace, truth and justice. Red is patriotism and courage.
quiz.objective: Read the symbolism of the Philippine flag

quiz.text: What does it mean when the flag is flown with red on top?
options: The country is in a state of war
quiz.explain: It is the only national flag designed to be flown two ways, and it is deliberate.
quiz.objective: Read the symbolism of the Philippine flag

quiz.text: The eight rays of the sun stand for eight national heroes.
quiz.explain: False. They stand for the first eight provinces that rose against Spain.
quiz.objective: Read the symbolism of the Philippine flag

quiz.text: What does good visual design usually do with elements?
options: Uses few, each carrying a clear meaning
Uses as many as will fit
quiz.explain: The flag has four elements and no words. It reads at any size and in one colour.
quiz.objective: Explain what a symbol is and how it differs from a picture

teacher.summary: Week 6 covers colour theory, symbolism and visual design, matching the MAPEH Arts scope. The colour wheel is taught with the actual colours on screen rather than named in text, which is the only honest way to teach it. The symbolism half is built on one distinction that generalises well beyond art: a sign that resembles its meaning versus one that works purely by agreement. The flag is the worked example, and the red-up convention is included because it is genuinely unusual and he is likely to remember it.
discussion: Ask him to find three symbols in the room that work by agreement rather than resemblance.
Ask why warning signs are red almost everywhere in the world.
Ask what would be lost if the flag had five more elements on it.
Ask him to name a game that teaches its controls through colour alone.
teacher.extension: Have him design a badge for something he cares about, using no more than three elements and two colours, then explain each choice in one sentence.
misconceptions: 'Red, green and blue are the primary colours.' That is for light on a screen. In paint it is red, yellow and blue.
'Warm and cool are just moods.' They change apparent distance, which is a measurable effect painters rely on.
'Complementary colours clash.' Side by side they intensify. It is mixing them that dulls both.
'The eight rays are eight islands.' They are the first eight provinces to revolt against Spain.
